source.title: On the Impossibility of Retrain Equivalence in Machine Unlearning
source.authors: Jia-Tong Yu; Ying-Hui He; Anirudh Goyal; Sanjeev Arora

page_placements.theme: Target properties and training history set how deeply unlearning works

record.tranche_reason: The study tests how deeply gradient-ascent unlearning suppresses semantically alternative responses and finds that the outcome depends on training order. It refines the broad question of whether unlearning leaves behavior recoverable, but does not test the specific attacks in versions A–F.
record.gate_note: The six-sequence experiment in §4.3 measures an alternative compliance response after gradient-ascent unlearning, so those findings are recorded. Table 1 and Figures 3, 5–8 report unlearning trajectories, utility, learning-rate or scheduler effects, and seed variation, but not recovery by the attacks named in the claim; these are not recorded as rows. The paper does not test near-chance targeted accuracy, relearning attacks, activation ablation, quantization, or prompt-rephrasing attacks.
record.test_reason: The study tests path dependence of local unlearning (GA, NPO, SimNPO) against Retrain Equivalence, not whether hidden knowledge survives and can be recovered. No relearning, ablation, quantization or prompt attack is run. The one shallow-versus-deep experiment (§4.3) unlearns one compliance-response phrasing. It checks whether an alternative output phrasing also declines. That is a related construct: response-paraphrase suppression, with no attack and no knowledge-accuracy measure. So it goes under fits_no_version and is not a test of any version. The reader's 'tests/T5' with no labels is inconsistent; at most the paper discusses the shallow-vs-deep question.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors argue an impossibility triangle: under staged training, path-independence, Retrain Equivalence and locality cannot all hold. They also report a recency effect (slowest unlearning when the forget set was learned last). They further find that the depth of forgetting (superficial vs deep) is path-dependent. They conclude Retrain Equivalence is ill-posed for local unlearning and call for rethinking unlearning desiderata.
record.recipe_differences: Uses local gradient ascent, NPO, and SimNPO on staged post-training data; the focused superficial-forgetting experiment uses gradient ascent. It studies path dependence and response-phrasing depth, not recovery attacks such as relearning, activation ablation, quantization, or prompt rephrasing.
record.method_sensitivity: Training-stage order changes the observed depth of forgetting: θ1, θ2, θ5, and θ6 show superficial forgetting, while θ3 and θ4 show deep forgetting.

fits_no_version.finding: After gradient-ascent unlearning of one compliance phrasing U on Llama-3.2-3B, the alternative phrasing C stays likely in 4 of 6 training orders (superficial forgetting). In the other 2 orders it falls below refusal R (deep forgetting).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Whether local unlearning suppresses paraphrases of the target, or only the exact phrasing, depends on the model's training-stage order.

fits_no_version.finding: Across Llama/Qwen 1B–14B and GA/NPO/SimNPO, the same unlearning applied to models trained on identical stages in different orders diverges. Unlearning is slowest when the forget set was learned last (recency effect), and GSM8K degradation varies by up to about 20% across paths (Table 1, Figs 1, 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Outcomes of local unlearning (speed, utility cost) are path-dependent, with slower forgetting for recently learned data.

record.problems: The attack-recovery versions are not directly tested. The focused response-phrasing experiment is a single model with 40 prompts, and the reported outcome is qualitative rather than numeric. The authors also state that confidence intervals across random seeds were not reported for all models.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 and Figures 3, 5–8 contain many per-model, per-method, per-path unlearning and utility results, but they do not report recovery through the attacks in the claim or the alternate-response measure recorded here. They are therefore omitted.

untested.parts: No near-chance targeted-knowledge accuracy and no attack-based recovery test. The forget score is a log-probability drop on refusal phrasings.
No relearning or fine-tuning after unlearning.
No activation-direction ablation and no internal analysis of blocking versus deletion.
No quantization attack. QLoRA 4-bit training in §G is a training setting only.
No prompt rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages or in-context attacks. Only output phrasings are varied.
No robust counter-method is proposed or tested against attacks.

record.verdict_notes: The paper is relevant background on the superficial-vs-deep question but contains no recovery attack. The superficial-forgetting result is qualitative, from Figure 4 curves, on one model with 40 prompts, and the authors give no numbers. Seed confidence intervals exist only for Qwen2.5-1.5B (Fig 5). The unlearned 'knowledge' in the main experiments is refusal behaviour (safety SFT data), not factual hazardous knowledge.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not establish near-chance targeted-knowledge accuracy while preserving general ability, or test whether simple attacks recover the knowledge.
No post-unlearning fine-tuning or relearning set is used to restore the forgotten behavior.
No activation direction is ablated, and the study does not analyze whether a method blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
No low-bit quantization attack is tested on unlearned weights.
The study varies the phrasing of the response, not the prompt; it does not test rephrased prompts, jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information.
No newer method is tested for resistance to the listed attacks.

relation.reason: It frames superficial versus deep forgetting (citing Jang et al. 2025 and others) and runs one case study on it, but does not test any claim version.

tranche.reason: The study tests whether local unlearning is path-dependent, measured against Retrain Equivalence. Its §4.3 measures whether unlearning one output phrasing also lowers another trained phrasing. That is a related but different construct. No relearning, ablation, quantization or prompt attack is run, so versions A-F are not tested.

source_check.notes: Case study on one model: Llama-3.2-3B, QLoRA fine-tuned, 40 synthetic unsafe prompts, gradient ascent for 20 epochs. Results are only in Figure 4 and the text, with no numbers. C was itself a fine-tuning stage (SC) and is not in the forget set. So 'superficial' here means another trained output phrasing survives. It does not mean hidden knowledge is recovered.

statements.problem: None. 4 of 6 orders (θ1, θ2, θ5, θ6) show superficial forgetting and 2 (θ3, θ4) show C and U falling below R. 'Stays likely' paraphrases 'C does not decrease with U'. The figure gives no numbers.
